newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Fox warns of peso "catastrophe".
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Fox warns of peso "catastrophe".

text.p: A leading opposition figure on Tuesday added his voice to a growing chorus of concern about the strength of Mexico's peso, warning the currency was overvalued and possibly headed for a new meltdown.

Vicente Fox, the charismatic governor of the central state of Guanajuato, took out full page ads in local newspapers on Tuesday warning the peso was too strong, as it was in 1994 before the government devalued the currency and touched off the country's worst economic crisis in 50 years.
"We don't want another economic catastrophe," said Fox, considered a rising star within the conservative National Action Party (PAN).
"All examples of overvaluation of our currency have ended in economic catastrophe. We ask the authorities to avoid a new blow to the economy that is already hurting," Fox said.
Fox said the peso was 2.4 percent overvalued, using 1990 as a base year and accounting for the differences in inflation between Mexico and the United States since that time.

After a spectacular crash in late 1994 and early 1995 that shook the world's financial markets, the peso has since steadied thanks to austere government economic programs and gained ground on the dollar, which itself has been strong against other currencies like the yen.

Since November 1995, the peso has traded at around 7.80 per dollar. But inflation in Mexico has been about 30 percent higher than that of the United States during that time, meaning the peso has gained in real terms.
One major difference this time around is that the market has set the price of the peso instead of policymakers, meaning many economists feel the currency is fairly valued.
"The degree of the Mexican peso's over- or undervaluation at any point in time is very much in the eyes of the beholder," said ING Barings in a recent report on the peso.

And few in Mexico expect a major crisis like the one in 1994, when the peso was fixed and overvalued by about 25-30 percent. But volatility in the peso could still hurt Mexico by pushing interest rates higher and dousing the first flames of an economic recovery.

The problem could be that the market has not worked perfectly. Foreign money has poured into Mexico's capital markets in the past few months and higher oil prices have helped boost dollar oil receipts for state oil company Petroleos Mexicanos.
Some politicians and economists worry the short-term, or "hot", foreign money could leave Mexico as it did in 1994.
And others, including Fox, fear a stronger peso will hurt Mexican exports, the most dynamic part of the economy, and add to Mexicans' appetite for imports.
Fox said on Tuesday that Mexico's trade balance excluding the in-bond, or maquiladora, industry is negative.
"Exporters are beginning to feel it is more difficult to maintain their presence in international markets," Fox said.
He did not specify, however, what actions he wanted the government to take to help keep the peso competitive.

Mexico's central bank, the Banco de Mexico, acted to address such concerns earlier this month by unveiling a new scheme to build reserves in times of peso strenth and stave off an unwelcome peso slump.
